Kashish: So how much will you charge for a poster?

Pankaj: I'm working it out. Let me write it down.

Kashish: Just say a number.

Pankaj: If I guess I'll lose money. Data for the design app, the bus to the print shop, two hours per poster. If I want a fair hour of my time, that's another chunk.

Kashish: And?

Pankaj: My first price of two hundred barely pays for data and travel. I'd be working for free.

Kashish: Wow. I would have said two hundred and been happy.

Pankaj: So did I, an hour ago. Now it's three fifty, and I can explain why.

Kashish: Do people pay that?

Pankaj: We'll see. At least I know my floor.

qa.q: What did the first price of two hundred barely cover?
qa.a: The first price of two hundred barely covered data and travel.

qa.q: What did Pankaj realise while working out the costs?
qa.a: Pankaj felt startled to realise that the first price left no pay for time, so the work would be free, and the price needed to change.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do if customers say three fifty is too high, and why?
qa.a: Pankaj could offer a simpler poster at a lower price, since the floor is known and the job can be trimmed.

qa.q: How might Kashish see the change from a guessed number to a worked one?
qa.a: Kashish may feel surprised and a bit impressed, since Kashish would have accepted two hundred without thinking.

grounding: A student works out costs, time per job and a fair hourly rate, and notices the first price barely covers data and travel.

subtype: Approach: budget and pricing with cost tracking [Thinking]
passage:
My name's Suraj, and last term I thought ₹200 a session for home maths tuition was good money. Then Elizabeth, who shares my table in the library, asked what I actually kept. I didn't know.
So I worked it out on the back of a lab sheet, half talking aloud. Auto both ways: ₹80. Mobile data for sending worksheets: roughly ₹20 a session. Printing: ₹10. That's ₹110 gone before I've taught anything. Each session is an hour, but with travel and preparing it's closer to two and a half. So I was earning about ₹36 an hour.
I stared at that number for a while. Elizabeth said, 'You're paying to teach.' Not quite, but close.
I've now asked the family to move two sessions a week online, and I'm working out what hourly rate would feel fair.

qa.q: What did the auto cost both ways?
How did Suraj feel on seeing the ₹36-an-hour figure?
qa.a: Suraj was shocked and a bit embarrassed, staring at the number, and then determined to rethink the setup.

qa.q: If you were Suraj, what would you change first?
qa.a: Cutting the travel, as Suraj did by moving sessions online, is a sensible first step; counting all hours and costs before agreeing any new job would help too.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Suraj's tuition work?
qa.a: Elizabeth sees plainly what Suraj missed: after costs the job barely pays, so Elizabeth sums it up with a blunt joke.

grounding: Shows a student working out costs, time per session and the real hourly earning, and noticing the price barely covers travel and data.

Mentoring note, Tuesday. Dolma, student enterprise cell.
Zainab came in with her mehendi plan: ₹300 per hand at weddings in her area. Before we discussed anything else, I asked her to list every cost. She did it at my desk, muttering as she wrote. 'Cones, ₹15 each, two a booking. Auto there and back, ₹150. Mobile data for sending design photos, say ₹30.' She paused. 'Mostly it's one hand per booking. Three hours with the travel.'
She added it herself. '₹300 in, ₹210 out. Ninety rupees for the whole evening.' She looked annoyed, then curious, and started drawing arrows on the page.
Next steps we agreed: she will price per event rather than per hand, and track real costs for her next three bookings. I will meet her again after the third one.

qa.q: How much did Zainab plan to charge per hand?
What was Zainab feeling when she worked out ninety rupees for the evening?
qa.a: She looked annoyed at first, then curious, as if the number stung but also made her want to fix the plan.

qa.q: What else could Zainab try so the work covers its costs?
qa.a: Besides pricing per event, she could group bookings in one area on the same day, so one auto trip serves several clients.

qa.q: How does the plan look to the mentor who wrote the note?
qa.a: The mentor sees a promising plan with a hidden gap and lets Zainab find it herself by listing costs, then sets a check-in after three bookings.

grounding: Shows a student listing costs and time per booking and seeing that the first price barely covers travel and data.
